title: Typing: resources cannot be assigned
objective: Write the five resource operations as posting pairs and the typing rules that forbid assigning a resource and demand a covering guard, then produce a command that a named rule rejects.

blocks.md: Your Stage 2 transfer had no assignment: it computed new balances from old ones, and every theorem followed from that. Give a language assignment and a command can write any number into a balance. This lesson is the set of rules that stops that before a command ever runs, and the two questions below are the ones those rules exist for.

choice.prompt: Draft 0 lets a command assign balances: `set balance(x) := e`. Which single command can mint money?

options.why: An assignment can write any value, so it can write one more than was there.

options.text: A transfer from an account to itself.
options.why: Sequential updates conserve on a self-transfer. Stage 2's mint came from computing both balances from the old state.

options.text: None: Transfer conserves, so the language conserves.
options.why: One conserving command says nothing about a language that also has assignment.

options.text: A transfer between two very large balances.
options.why: Lean's `Int` does not overflow.

choice.prompt: Amounts are plain `Int`. Which guarded command can drive an account negative?

options.text: `move amount from from to to` under `requires balance(from) >= amount`, with amount -5.
options.why: A negative move debits `to`, and no guard mentions `to`.

options.text: None: the guard checks the balance.
options.why: A guard covers the account it names, not the other one.

options.text: Only a transfer from an account to itself.
options.why: A positive self-transfer nets to zero.

blocks.md:
A typing judgment says when a command is well-formed, before any state exists. It is written Γ ⊢ c ok: in a context Γ that lists the parameters and their types, the command c is accepted. This course writes it as a function, `typecheck : Ctx → Cmd → Except TypeErr Unit`, and defines `HasType Γ c` as `typecheck Γ c = .ok ()`. Every rejection then names the rule that fired, and a rule you got wrong shows up as a failing check you can read.[^1]

[^1]: Harper's *Practical Foundations for Programming Languages*, chapter 4, draws the same rules as inference rules.

| Rule | Requires | Rejection | Protects |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-param | distinct parameter names, each with a declared type | `dupParam` | well-formedness |
| R-var | every variable is a parameter | `unknownParam` | well-formedness |
| R-expr | `balance(e)` and `frozen(e)` take an account; arithmetic and `>=` take numbers; the guard is a bool | `wrongType` | no expression gets stuck |
| R-cover | a `move n from x ...` or `hold n on x` needs a top-level guard conjunct `balance(x) >= n` | `unguardedDebit` | non-negativity of the debited account |

R-cover is the rule that ties a guard to a body. `Covers g x n` holds when `g` is `balance(x) >= n`, or when `g` is `g₁ && g₂` and either side covers. A disjunction never covers. The rule is sound and incomplete: `balance(x) >= n + fee` implies coverage without covering syntactically, and Stage 4's obligations prove what the rule cannot see.

```lean
/-- `covers g x n`: some top-level conjunct of `g` is `balance(x) >= n`. -/
def covers : Expr → Expr → Expr → Bool
  | .ge (.balance y) m, x, n => y == x && m == n
  | .and g₁ g₂,         x, n => covers g₁ x n || covers g₂ x n
  | _,                  _, _ => false

/-- The R-cover clause of `typecheck`: a debit needs a covering guard. -/
def checkBody (g : Expr) : Stmt → Except TypeErr Unit
  | .op (.move n x _) => if covers g x n then .ok () else .error .unguardedDebit
  | .op (.hold n x)   => if covers g x n then .ok () else .error .unguardedDebit
  | _                 => .ok ()
```

blocks.direction: The typing view walks the command once and shows either its derivation or the rule that fails. No state is involved.

code.text:
command Pay(from: account, to: account, amount: amount)
  requires balance(to) >= amount
  do move amount from from to to

options.why: R-cover also asks which account the guard protects.

options.text: No: the guard does not cover the debited account.
options.why: R-cover needs `balance(from) >= amount`, and this guard names the credited account.
`to` is an account, so `balance(to)` is well-typed.

blocks.after: R-var and R-expr both pass: `to` and `amount` are parameters, and `balance(to) >= amount` is a bool. Then R-cover looks for a conjunct that names the debited account, `from`, and finds only `to`, so the rule that fires is `unguardedDebit` {{run:RUN-lean-golden-harness}}. No balance was needed: the text of the command is enough to see that it can overdraw `from`.

choice.prompt: Which edit to the roadmap's `Transfer` makes the reference typechecker reject it with `unguardedDebit`? Then say what that rule protects.

options.why: The original conjunct still covers `from`. R-cover asks for some conjunct, not for the whole guard.

options.text: Change the body to `move amount from to to from`.
options.why: The body now debits `to`, and no conjunct names `to`. R-cover protects the debited account's non-negativity.
This is rejected, but by R-expr as `wrongType`, because `balance` takes an account.

blocks.md:
An operation never edits a balance. It posts a pair of entries: a debit from one account and a credit of the same amount to another, so every operation is zero-sum. `mint` is the account that creates money, `sink` absorbs it, and a hold parks money in an escrow account. Write `bal s x` for the balance of account `x` in state `s`.

| Operation | Postings (debit to credit) | Run-time checks |
|---|---|---|
| `deposit n to a` | `mint` to `a` | `a` exists |
| `move n from x to y` | `x` to `y` | `x` and `y` exist |
| `hold n on x` | `x` to escrow `h` | `x` exists; `h` is the next hold number |
| `capture h to y` | escrow `h` to `y` | the hold exists, is open and is covered |
| `release h` | escrow `h` to the hold's owner | the same |

The invariant `Inv` says that keys are unique, the total of all balances is 0, and every account except `mint` is non-negative. A zero-sum pair keeps the total at 0 whatever a guard says, so conservation costs no proof per command. Only a debit can push a balance below zero, so non-negativity is the per-command obligation: R-cover pays it for `move` and `hold`, and a run-time check pays it for `capture` and `release`.

Three more rules keep a command from sidestepping the pairs.

| Rule | Requires | Rejection | Protects |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-set | `set f(x) := e` needs a scalar field `f`; `balance` is a resource and has no assignment rule | `assignsResource` | conservation |
| R-amount | an operation's amount is an `amount` parameter or a positive literal | `nonPositive` | the direction of every posting |
| R-hold | `capture h to y` and `release h` need `h : hold`, and `y : account` or `sink` | `wrongType` | no stuck statement |

R-amount matters because `move -5 from x to y` credits `x` and debits `y`, and no guard mentions `y`.
Three operations in a row, from a small state.
blocks.direction: The posting view lists the balances before and after each step. `h` is the hold that step 1 creates.

code.text:
start    mint -100 · a 100 · sink 0
1   hold 30 on a
2   capture h to sink
3   release h

call.prompt: After `hold 30 on a` and `capture h to sink`, what does `release h` do?

options.why: Capture emptied the escrow and closed the hold.
A run-time check refuses a second resolution. No typechecker knows a hold's status.

options.text: It is rejected before it runs, as ill-typed.
options.why: `release h` with `h : hold` is well-typed. This is a run-time outcome.

blocks.after: Every step moved money in pairs, so the total stayed at 0 throughout. The third step was refused at run time, as `holdNotOpen`, because the hold was already resolved {{run:RUN-lean-golden-harness}}. A typechecker reads a command, and a hold's status lives in the state, so no typing rule can make this check. Your own system draws the same line: a missing check is visible in the code, and an already-resolved hold is visible only in the data.

choice.prompt: A variant checker drops R-set. Which command does it now accept, and which part of `Inv` does the command break?

options.why: The total becomes 1, and no posting pair balances it.
The balance grew, so it did not go negative. The total is what changed.

options.text: `move 5 from a to b` under `requires balance(a) >= 5`, which breaks non-negativity.
options.why: The guard covers the debit, so both checkers accept it and `Inv` holds.

options.text: `move 5 from a to a`, which breaks conservation.
options.why: A self-move debits and credits one account, so the total is unchanged.

blocks.md:
R-amount asks every amount to be positive, and a type can promise that once instead of each operation checking it. A subtype packs a value with a proof: `Amount := {n : Int // 0 < n}` is an integer together with a proof that it is positive. Lean checks the proof when the value is built, and no operation has to look again. Values of Mini-Plinth's `amount` type are `Amount`s.

Raw input is the catch. A call arrives with plain integers, and the boundary that decodes them has to build an `Amount` from each one.

blocks.direction: Goal Replay shows the goal at each step: the proof of positivity that a value must carry.

code.text:
abbrev Amount := { n : Int // 0 < n }

example : Amount := ⟨30, by decide⟩    -- goal: 0 < 30

example : Amount := ⟨0, by decide⟩     -- goal: 0 < 0

def Amount.add (a b : Amount) : Amount :=
  ⟨a.val + b.val, by
    have ha := a.property
    have hb := b.property
    omega⟩

call.prompt: Can the boundary turn the argument 0 into an `Amount`?

options.text: No: there is no proof of `0 < 0`, so the boundary must reject zero or treat it specially.
options.why: A subtype value carries its proof, checked once at construction. Zero becomes a boundary decision.

options.text: Yes: Lean raises an error later, when the amount is used.
options.why: There is no later check. The value cannot be built at all.

blocks.after: `decide` tries to prove `0 < 0` and reports that the proposition is false {{run:RUN-lean-golden-harness}}. The proof is part of the value, so no zero `Amount` exists to catch later. What the boundary does with a zero argument is a decision, and you make it in S3.L7. The third step, `Amount.add`, uses the proofs both inputs carry, which `omega` combines.

choice.prompt: In S3.L6 you prove `move_inv`: a successful `move n from x to y` from a state with `Inv s` gives a state with `Inv`. Which hypothesis does the proof need to show the credited account stays non-negative?

options.why: The credit adds `n`, and the sum stays non-negative only if `n` is.
A self-move changes nothing and is fine, so the proof does not need it.
`Inv` says nothing about frozen flags.
This pays for the debited account, not the credited one.

choice.prompt: The reference typechecker rejects `command Grab(a: account, amount: amount) requires frozen(a) do hold amount on a`. Which rule fired?

options.text: R-expr: a guard must be a bool.
options.why: `frozen(a)` is a bool, so R-expr passes.

options.text: R-cover: no conjunct of the guard is `balance(a) >= amount`.
options.why: `hold` debits `a`, and the guard never mentions its balance.
R-var is about variables, and `a` is a parameter.

options.text: None: a frozen check is a good guard for a hold.
options.why: A guard protects only the account and the amount it names.

choice.prompt: A variant checker keeps R-set but drops R-amount. Which command does it accept that breaks `Inv`?

options.text: `move -5 from a to b` under `requires balance(a) >= -5`
options.why: It credits `a` and debits `b`, and no guard mentions `b`, so `b` can go negative.
It credits `a` and debits `mint`, which `Inv` exempts.
The guard covers the debit, so both checkers accept it and `Inv` holds.

options.text: `move 5 from a to a` under `requires balance(a) >= 5`
options.why: A self-move changes nothing.

choice.prompt: In `deposit_inv`, `deposit n to a` posts from `mint` to `a`. Besides `Inv s`, which hypothesis does the proof need for `a` to stay non-negative?

options.why: The credit adds `n`, so `n` must be non-negative.
`mint` is exempt from non-negativity, so no coverage is needed.
Posting from `mint` to `mint` changes nothing, so the proof does not need it.
`Inv` says nothing about frozen flags.

blocks.title: Production twin
blocks.md: TigerBeetle's two-phase transfers: a pending transfer reserves an amount, and a later post or void resolves it. Read its documentation of two-phase transfers, pinned in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}, and match pending, post and void to `hold`, `capture` and `release`. Then ask what stops a second resolution.
